stories.headline: Update: Barry Morphew arrested after GPS data reveals bond violations tied to Denver hit-and-run
stories.summary:
Boulder County sheriff's deputies arrested murder suspect Barry Morphew on Thursday night on an Alamosa County bench warrant after prosecutors alleged he violated his bail conditions by traveling around metro Denver for non-work purposes. The 58-year-old had been under a $3 million bail agreement requiring him to leave home only for medical appointments, emergencies, legal meetings and work while awaiting trial on first-degree murder charges in the death of his wife, Suzanne Morphew.

The violations came to light after Morphew was involved in a hit-and-run crash in Denver on Aug. 26, in which he allegedly drove aggressively, struck two vehicles and refused to identify himself. Prosecutors reviewed GPS data from his ankle monitor and found he had traveled to Denver International Airport, driven near hotels and a mall, and visited the crash site near East Eighth Avenue and Colorado Boulevard.

Alamosa County District Court Chief Judge Amanda Hopkins had already modified Morphew's bail mid-week to restrict him to home except for medical emergencies. After issuing the arrest warrant Thursday, she further adjusted bail to $3 million cash-only. A bond hearing is scheduled for Tuesday.

Morphew was originally charged with his wife's murder in 2021; that case was dismissed after prosecutorial misconduct. Suzanne Morphew's body was found in a shallow grave near Moffat in 2023, and Barry Morphew was recharged with her murder in June 2025. His jury trial is scheduled for July 2027.

stories.headline: Denver church sued for failing to report music director's sexual assault of 13-year-old girl
stories.summary:
The parents of a 13-year-old girl who was sexually assaulted by a music director at St. John's Church and School in Denver in 2022 filed a lawsuit Friday against the institution, alleging church leaders violated Colorado's mandatory reporting laws. The complaint, brought by Denver law firm Rathod Mohamedbhai, alleges that lead pastor Andrew Farhat not only failed to report the assault to authorities but pressured the girl into recanting her allegations during a meeting that included the accused, Diego Marroquin.

According to the lawsuit, Marroquin, then a music director at the school on South Franklin Street, got the 13-year-old alone after school and sexually assaulted her in the church balcony in May 2022. The girl later became pregnant and secretly obtained abortion pills. Voice memos from June 2022 allegedly show Marroquin referencing a 'relationship' with the teenager.

Church leaders became aware of the allegations in August 2022. Rather than contacting authorities, Farhat called the girl, her father and Marroquin into his office, chastised the girl for spreading what he called false rumors, told her to seek forgiveness and ordered her to stay silent, according to the complaint. The girl's parents ultimately took the matter to police themselves.

Marroquin was charged with felony sex assault on a child and later pleaded guilty to contributing to the delinquency of a minor — a felony — and misdemeanor assault. He was required to register as a sex offender and was subsequently deported to Guatemala. Farhat did not return a request for comment Friday.

stories.headline: NTSB investigating crash that killed five teenage boys when car plunged off Grand Junction cliff
stories.summary:
The National Transportation Safety Board has opened an investigation into a crash that killed five 17-year-old boys when a 2003 Cadillac CTS drove off the edge of a cliff in Grand Junction on Aug. 8. A preliminary federal report released this week found the driver failed to negotiate a leftward curve on Lookout Lane just before midnight, sending the vehicle off the road, down a steep embankment and over a cliff into the rocks above the Gunnison River below.

The Mesa County Coroner's Office identified the five victims as Tristan Tucker, William Simms, Tyler Kersey-Huffman, Titus Gould and Braden Taylor, all of whom died in the crash. Federal investigators described the roadway as two lanes with multiple curves and dry conditions at the time of the incident.

NTSB's preliminary report included photos showing tire tracks where the vehicle left the road, crossed a sidewalk and a lawn before going over the cliff. The agency said all aspects of the crash remain under investigation as it works to determine probable cause.

Federal investigators typically publish final crash reports, including probable cause and contributing factors, between 12 and 24 months after a crash. The agency intends to issue safety recommendations aimed at preventing similar tragedies.

stories.headline: Colorado kills 294 bears in 2026, more than three times last year's total, amid drought and wildfire
stories.summary:
Colorado Parks and Wildlife has euthanized 294 black bears through Aug. 31, compared with 83 during the same period last year, the agency announced Friday in an early release driven by high public interest. The surge in bear deaths mirrors a dramatic rise in human-bear conflicts, with 8,672 incidents reported so far in 2026 versus 3,680 through August of 2025.

Drought and wildfire have depleted the bears' natural food sources — primarily berries and acorns — at a time when the animals need up to 20,000 calories per day to prepare for hibernation. As natural forage disappears, bears increasingly seek food near homes, businesses and roads, raising the likelihood of dangerous encounters and vehicle strikes. In Garfield County alone, 39 bears have been put down after being hit by cars, compared to just one at this point last year.

CPW officers follow an escalating response scale. A single bear near trash does not automatically trigger a visit, but a bear repeatedly entering homes or attacking residents indoors can lead to euthanasia. This year, 98 bears have been relocated compared with 33 at the same point in 2025.

The numbers far exceed the five-year average on every metric: incidents are up 3.6 times, relocations 3.5 times and euthanizations 2.7 times. Officials said a plant-killing late-May freeze in some areas, combined with record heat in others, has compounded the effects of drought in pushing bears into closer contact with people.

stories.headline: CBI affirms Boulder County's investigation into CU student Megan Trussell's death, family seeks more answers
stories.summary:
The Colorado Bureau of Investigation on Friday announced it has completed a review of the Boulder County investigation into the death of University of Colorado student Megan Trussell and found the local response 'reasonable, substantial and supported by the available evidence.' Trussell, 18, went missing from her campus dorm on Feb. 9, 2025, and her body was found Feb. 15 in rugged terrain near the Elephant Buttress trailhead in Boulder Canyon.

The Boulder County coroner ruled Trussell's death a suicide resulting from the toxic effects of amphetamines and hypothermia. Her family rejected that finding and petitioned the state attorney general's office for an outside review. The CBI launched its investigation in January under a 2022 law requiring state review of certain cases involving Indigenous people.

CBI Director Armando Saldate III said the review examined the entire investigative record, including digital evidence, cellular analysis, campus access records, body-camera video, search records and forensic files. The case was also presented to the agency's cold case review team in July, a panel that included about 40 prosecutors, investigators, toxicologists, analysts, victims advocates and forensic pathologists.

The agency did not release a copy of its full review Friday. Trussell's family said they still have more questions than answers about her death. Saldate acknowledged that 'no administrative review can undo the profound loss experienced by the Trussell family or answer every remaining question.'

stories.headline: Climber dies in Maroon Bells wilderness; body recovery delayed by technical terrain
stories.summary:
Search and rescue teams located the body of a climber who died in the Maroon Bells-Snowmass Wilderness southwest of Aspen, the Pitkin County Sheriff's Office announced Friday. The climber was reported overdue Wednesday, and a Mountain Rescue Aspen member flying with CareFlight of the Rockies located the body Thursday during an aerial search.

Authorities said they did not know the climber's intended route or itinerary but found notes in the person's rental car related to climbing the Maroon Bells. The U.S. Forest Service closed Maroon Peak to allow recovery crews to work the area. Because of the extremely technical terrain, recovery operations are not expected to begin until Tuesday.

The Maroon Bells are 14,000-foot peaks known for their distinctive bell-shaped summits above Maroon Lake. Maroon Peak at 14,163 feet is widely considered among the most difficult and dangerous standard 14er routes, with high exposure, significant rockfall risk and challenging route-finding.

The sheriff's office said the climber's name will be released after the body is recovered and the family has been notified. Officials used the incident to remind backcountry travelers to leave detailed itineraries with trusted contacts before heading out and to carry the ten essentials recommended by the Colorado Search and Rescue Association.

stories.headline: Metro Denver home sales fall nearly 20% in August as mortgage rates and economic uncertainty weigh on buyers
stories.summary:
Metro Denver home sales fell by nearly a fifth between July and August, with buyers closing on only 3,068 properties last month — a volume more typical of cold-weather holiday periods than the height of summer, according to the Denver Metro Association of Realtors. The 17.3% annual decline in sales cannot be attributed to seasonal patterns alone, DMAR Market Trends Committee chairwoman Amanda Snitker said.

Stubbornly elevated mortgage rates hovering closer to 7% than 6%, persistent inflation and shifting tariff policies are all generating uncertainty among potential buyers, Snitker said. The condo and townhome segment showed particular weakness, with a 23.5% annual decline in sales and a median sold price of $370,000 in August — down 2.6% from July and nearly 5% from a year earlier.

Despite the sales slowdown, inventory and single-family prices remained relatively stable. The number of homes and condos for sale stood at 13,080, barely changed from July and roughly flat compared to a year ago. Sellers listed about 10% fewer properties in August than July, helping prevent a glut of unsold homes from building up. The median single-family home sold for $649,500, down just 1.65% from July.

Some analysts are sounding louder alarms. Nick Gerli of real estate data platform Reventure Consulting is predicting home price declines of 10% to 20% in some areas, saying Denver rivals Austin, Texas, as the nation's most distressed metro housing market. He argues that a wave of investor-owned properties purchased during the 2020-2022 buying frenzy is coming under increasing pressure to sell, which could accelerate price declines heading into winter.

stories.headline: Colorado judge allows Libertarian Party to replace secretary of state candidate after suspicious late dropout
stories.summary:
A Denver District Court judge ruled Friday that Colorado's Libertarian Party can place a replacement candidate on November's ballot for secretary of state after the party's original nominee dropped out one day past the deadline for an automatic swap. Denver District Judge Adam J. Espinosa found the Libertarians had substantially complied with election rules and that adding the new candidate would not impede the Secretary of State's Office from finalizing the ballot, which was due Friday.

The episode centered on Alex Astley, a political newcomer and electrical engineer from Holyoke, who withdrew from the race Aug. 26 — 69 days before the Nov. 3 election — missing the 70-day cutoff by one day. Astley's late exit fueled suspicion within the Libertarian Party that he had intentionally withdrawn to benefit James Wiley, a former Libertarian running as a Republican in the same race. Astley denied any coordination, saying he was busy and had not fully considered the timing implications of his withdrawal.

The party quickly named Sean Vadney as Astley's replacement, meeting the separate 64-day deadline for requesting a substitution. When the Secretary of State's Office denied the swap because Astley had missed the first deadline, both the Libertarians and the Secretary of State asked the court to decide. Espinosa ruled that blocking Vadney would disenfranchise Colorado's approximately 33,000 active Libertarian voters.

The judge cited a principle he described as 'the tie goes to the voter,' favoring a liberal interpretation of election rules that prioritizes ballot access. Libertarian attorney Nicholas Sarwark praised the ruling. Astley's campaign motto had been a play on Rick Astley's 1980s hit; some party members now say he 'Rickrolled' them with his withdrawal.

stories.headline: Motorcyclist seriously injured in crash on South University Boulevard near DU campus
stories.summary:
A motorcyclist suffered serious injuries Thursday evening in a single-vehicle crash at South University Boulevard and East Warren Avenue, near the University of Denver campus, prompting Denver Police to shut down northbound University Boulevard as investigators worked the scene. The closure was announced just after 9 p.m., leaving drivers in the area scrambling for alternate routes.

Denver Police did not release the rider's name, age or condition, and said the cause of the crash remained under investigation. The department issues public Crash Alerts only when a collision involves at least one person with serious injuries or requires a road closure — thresholds this crash met on both counts.

The stretch of road is part of Denver's High Injury Network, a designation covering roughly 5% of city roadway mileage that accounts for about half of all local traffic fatalities and serious injuries. A motorcyclist died in June after colliding with an SUV on South University Boulevard near East Floyd Avenue, approximately two miles south of Thursday's crash site.

Motorcycle fatalities in Colorado hit a record 165 in 2024, accounting for nearly 24% of all traffic deaths statewide despite motorcycles making up only 3% of registered vehicles. The early months of 2026 saw 15 motorcycle fatalities in the first quarter alone — the deadliest start to a year for riders since 2017 — before the pace eased heading into summer.

stories.headline: Colorado Bat Watch program enlists volunteers to track bat populations as deadly white-nose syndrome spreads
stories.summary:
A community science program called Colorado Bat Watch is enlisting volunteers across the state to count and document bats as they emerge from mines, bridges, buildings and other roost sites, with the goal of establishing population baselines to guide conservation efforts. The program, launched in 2023 by the nonprofit Rocky Mountain Wild, has so far engaged about 100 volunteers observing bat habitats primarily in Boulder County, with observation spots filling within minutes of opening.

The data is especially critical as white-nose syndrome — a fast-moving fungal disease that has killed millions of bats across North America — continues to spread into Colorado. Of approximately 20 bat species living in the state, scientists say they know relatively little about where most of them roost or how their numbers are changing over time.

Conservation biologist Megan Mueller said bats can roost in an enormous variety of locations, from high alpine forests to downtown Denver buildings, making population surveys logistically difficult. Maternity roosts — where female bats give birth and raise their young — are considered particularly vital sites to monitor because losing them can devastate local populations.

Volunteers have traveled from as far as Kansas to participate in observation sessions. Program leaders say they hope to expand Colorado Bat Watch to additional sites across the state, using the accumulated data to help protect bat habitat before white-nose syndrome takes a broader toll on Colorado's populations.

stories.headline: Rockies face Cardinals tonight after snapping franchise-record 10-game home losing streak
stories.summary:
The Colorado Rockies enter Saturday's home game against the St. Louis Cardinals coming off a 4-2 victory over the Baltimore Orioles that ended the franchise's longest home losing streak on record at 10 games. TJ Rumfield broke a seventh-inning tie with a two-run home run to secure the win Tuesday night.

Despite the morale-boosting victory, Colorado's broader season struggles remain stark. The Rockies stand at 54-86, the second-worst record in Major League Baseball, one game better than the Los Angeles Angels. The team is widely expected to hold a high draft pick position again next offseason.

Colorado enters tonight's divisional matchup against St. Louis having gone 4-6 over its last 10 games. The Cardinals series represents a chance to build on the momentum from ending the historic home skid.

The Rockies have been in rebuilding mode for several seasons, with a farm system focused on developing young talent. Results at the major league level have remained difficult as the organization works toward long-term competitiveness.

stories.headline: Avalanche 2026-27 season preview: Makar contract secured, Nichushkin traded, MacKinnon seeking redemption
stories.summary:
The Colorado Avalanche enter the 2026-27 season with their defensive cornerstone locked in after securing Cale Makar's contract, but the roster has undergone significant changes that will test the team's depth heading into the new campaign. Forward Valeri Nichushkin has been traded, removing a key complementary piece from the lineup that helped anchor Colorado's forward corps in recent seasons.

Nathan MacKinnon, widely regarded as one of the NHL's premier players, enters the season with a redemption narrative after the Avalanche fell short of their championship expectations in 2025-26. The two-time Stanley Cup champion center is expected to carry a heavy offensive load alongside Makar on the back end.

Colorado's front office faces questions about how the roster shake-up affects the team's championship window. Makar's contract security provides long-term stability on the blue line, but replacing Nichushkin's production will require contributions from younger forwards or free-agent additions.

The Avalanche have been one of the Western Conference's top teams since their 2022 Stanley Cup title, and expectations remain high in Denver despite the roster turnover. The 2026-27 regular season will test whether the team can maintain its competitive standing through the transition.

topStory.headline: Trump Calls Iran Conflict 'Small Potatoes' as Explosions Reported Near Key Oil Hub
topStory.summary:
President Donald Trump downplayed the ongoing U.S.-Iran military conflict Friday, telling reporters in the Oval Office that he considers it a "military conflict" rather than a war, describing it as "small potatoes for us." Trump also claimed there was "no fighting right now" despite a sharp escalation in hostilities this week involving U.S. strikes on Iran, and said the United States controls the Strait of Hormuz — a claim that does not accurately reflect current conditions.

Separately, Iranian state media reported multiple explosions Saturday near Kharg Island, the country's major oil hub in the Persian Gulf. The Fars news agency confirmed its correspondent heard blasts but reported no visible smoke, while the SNN news agency claimed a U.S. strike targeted an Iranian tanker near the island. The reports have not been independently verified.

The conflict, which began in late February, has resulted in 18 U.S. service member deaths, more than 750 American troops wounded, and thousands of Iranian casualties. The war has also driven gas prices to record highs and disrupted global food supply chains, as a blockade over the Strait of Hormuz has severely restricted international trade and oil shipments. Trump's characterization of the conflict as "small potatoes" drew immediate attention given that he has himself repeatedly referred to it as a war, including calling it "a relatively little war" just days earlier on Monday.

On the diplomatic front, the United States, Britain, France, and Germany have drafted a resolution for consideration by the Board of Governors of the International Atomic Energy Agency that would refer Iran to the U.N. Security Council for failing to comply with its nuclear nonproliferation obligations. The draft resolution follows an IAEA board finding in June 2025 — the first such finding in 20 years — that Iran was in noncompliance, a determination made one day before the U.S. and Israel launched strikes on Iranian nuclear sites. The resolution is expected to go to a vote at next week's IAEA board meeting in Vienna.

Practical enforcement through the U.N. Security Council is considered unlikely, however, as Russia and China — both allies of Iran — hold veto power on the council. In a separate development, the U.S. State Department on Friday approved a $5 billion arms sale to Saudi Arabia, which has faced repeated attacks during the conflict, citing the need to bolster Saudi airborne defense capabilities and regional interoperability with U.S. forces. Trump also said Friday that the U.S. could strike Iran's Pickaxe Mountain nuclear facilities "very soon."
